title: What real-time substrate serves text chat first and grows to voice, recording and transcripts - legally?
summary: DO WebSockets with hibernation (the existing /imagine/stream/doc/durable-objects.md), presence and fan-out limits, chat history storage, Cloudflare Realtime / WebRTC for voice, recording and transcription costs, consent law, retention, live moderation. MVP is text only.

title: DO pricing re-verified 2026-09-04: unchanged from durable-objects.md
summary: Requests USD0.15/M beyond 1M/mo free; WS inbound bills 20:1, outbound free; Duration USD12.50/M GB-s beyond 400,000 GB-s/mo free, metered at fixed 128MB; SQLite USD0.001/M rows read, USD1.00/M rows written beyond 25B/50M free; storage USD0.20/GB-mo beyond 5GB free. Every number matches durable-objects.md exactly. Re-fetched 2026-09-04.

title: Free-plan storage 5GB vs 1GB is not a contradiction: account vs per-object
summary: durable-objects.md flagged the limits page as self-contradicting (5GB in the table, 1GB in the FAQ). Resolved 2026-09-04: 5GB is the Free plan's account-wide total; 1GB is the per-object cap on Free (a footnote); 10GB per object is the Paid-plan cap. Two different scopes, not a contradiction. The doc's caveat can be removed.

title: 32,768 WS connections per DO confirmed, still only on the api/state page
summary: acceptWebSocket() docs, re-fetched 2026-09-04: the Hibernation API 'permits a maximum of 32,768 WebSocket connections per Durable Object, but the CPU and memory usage of a given workload may further limit the practical number.' Matches durable-objects.md's citation exactly; the dedicated limits page still does not carry this number.

title: CF's own worked example: hibernating USD20.65/mo vs non-hibernating USD142.95/mo
summary: Official pricing page, Example 4: 100 DOs, 100 hibernatable connections each, 1 msg/min/socket, 10ms processing = 432M msgs/mo -> USD3.15 requests + USD12.50 duration + USD5 min = USD20.65/mo. Example 2, same traffic without hibernation (plain addEventListener): USD142.95/mo. Confirms durable-objects.md's cited figures almost exactly (it rounded to ~USD142).

title: Modeled fan-out cost, one room: 100/1k/10k sockets, light activity
summary: Using CF's own per-message rate (10ms/msg incl. broadcast, ~1 msg/min/user) applied to ONE DO instead of 100: request cost stays near-free at all three sizes -- even 10k users x 1msg/min = 432M msgs/mo gives ~21.6M billed requests, about USD3/mo. Duration is the open question: CF never varies the fan-out target size in its own example, so whether 10ms/msg still holds broadcasting to 10,000 sockets instead of 100 is not documented. This is my extrapolation, not a published number.

title: No published benchmark: does per-message DO cost scale with room size
summary: CF's worked pricing examples fix connection count at 100 and never test whether the assumed 10ms/message processing time holds when a message fans out to 1,000 or 10,000 sockets instead. If per-message cost scales with recipient count, a single very chatty large room risks O(N) messages x O(N) fanout = O(N^2) work, which could hit the ~1,000 req/sec soft overload limit well before 10k concurrent users. Nobody has published a real benchmark at that scale; this is the strongest technical argument for capping room size rather than trusting the DO to absorb it.

title: One DO per channel, not per topic: CF's own anti-pattern rule applies
summary: CF names 'never route all traffic through one Durable Object instance' as the anti-pattern to avoid. Brief SS18 says a topic may contain many channels (text, voice, wiki, docs, subtopics). Routing all of a topic's channels through one object would serialize every channel's fan-out through one ~1,000 req/sec soft limit and one 32,768-connection cap, and a single deploy would drop every channel in the topic at once. Recommend one DO per channel/room, keyed by channel id. This is my architectural argument built on an established CF rule, not itself CF guidance -- contested because CF never addresses multi-channel topics directly.

title: Socket.js confirms the doc's one-url claim; row-id swap needs no client parsing change
summary: connect() builds the WebSocket url from window.location.host in exactly one place (public/framework/dev/Socket/Socket.js line 54). Pointing at a DO's url instead is a one-line change. wire.md confirms subscribe's from and jsonl's trailing offset are opaque server-issued values the client only echoes back, never computes -- so a DO handing back a row id instead of a byte offset needs zero client-side parsing change. Verified by reading both files 2026-09-04.

title: Hibernation is WebSocket-only in Durable Objects -- SSE does not get the discount
summary: Direct quote, best-practices/websockets page: 'Hibernation is only supported when a Durable Object acts as a WebSocket server. Outgoing WebSockets do not hibernate.' No mention anywhere of a plain HTTP streaming response (SSE) hibernating. An SSE connection held open in a DO keeps the isolate pinned in memory and bills full Duration for the whole session -- the USD142.95/mo non-hibernating scenario, not the USD20.65/mo one.

title: Answering the challenge: WebSockets beat SSE+POST for a DO text-first MVP
summary: Because hibernation is WebSocket-only (see the paired finding), an SSE+POST design in a Durable Object cannot get the hibernation discount that makes chat nearly free when idle -- every open SSE connection bills Duration continuously, the non-hibernating USD142.95/mo shape, regardless of message volume. WebSockets with the Hibernation API is the only path to the USD20.65/mo shape. This is my inference chained from an established CF statement, not itself stated by CF as a recommendation against SSE.

title: Cloudflare Realtime SFU/TURN: USD0.05/GB egress, 1000GB free/mo, no per-minute price
summary: Pricing page (dated 2026-04-21, re-fetched 2026-09-04): '1,000 GB before any charges start' free, then USD0.05 per GB of data egress from Cloudflare edge to your application, for both SFU and TURN. 'Traffic between Cloudflare Realtime TURN and SFU or Stream (WHIP/WHEP) does not get double charged.' No per-minute or per-participant charge at this layer -- billing is flat per-GB egress, unlike every competitor below.

title: RealtimeKit per-minute pricing: USD0.002/min AV, USD0.0005/min audio-only
summary: RealtimeKit pricing page, last updated 2026-09-03 (yesterday), fetched 2026-09-04: Audio/Video participant USD0.002/min; Audio-only participant USD0.0005/min; Export (recording/RTMP/HLS) USD0.010/min, audio-only USD0.003/min; Export (Raw RTP) into R2 USD0.0005/min; real-time transcription billed at standard Workers AI model pricing.

title: RealtimeKit free-beta-vs-priced: sources disagree on current status
summary: Multiple 2026 blog summaries describe RealtimeKit as 'currently in Beta and free to use.' The primary pricing page itself, dated 2026-09-03, presents per-minute pricing as the active commercial model with no beta/free notice and links a cost calculator. Either the page went live with real pricing very recently, or third-party writeups have not caught up. Recommend treating it as priced, not free, for planning.

title: LiveKit Cloud: WebRTC USD0.0004-0.0005/participant-min, tiered plans USD0-500/mo
summary: livekit.com/pricing, fetched 2026-09-04. Build (USD0/mo): 5,000 WebRTC participant-min included then USD0.0005/min, 60 recording/egress min included. Ship (USD50/mo): 150,000 min included then USD0.0005/min, USD0.02/min video recording, USD0.005/min audio. Scale (USD500/mo): 1.5M min included then USD0.0004/min. Track egress USD0.001/min beyond included.

title: Daily.co: USD0.004/participant-min video, USD0.00099/min audio-only, 10k free
summary: daily.co/pricing/webrtc-infrastructure, fetched 2026-09-04: 10,000 free participant-minutes/month, then USD0.0040/participant-minute for video/audio calls, USD0.00099/minute for audio-only. Cloud recording USD0.01349/recorded-minute plus USD0.003/min storage. Volume discounts to ~USD0.0015/min at 50M+ minutes/month.

title: Agora voice calling: USD0.00099/min, 10,000 free minutes/month
summary: agora.io/en/pricing/voice-calling, fetched 2026-09-04: 'USD0.99 / 1,000 minutes' = USD0.00099/minute for voice-only, with a 10,000-minute/month free bucket shared across products (excluding Conversational AI, which is separately priced at USD0.10/min after 300 free min).

title: Flat per-GB egress (Realtime SFU) beats per-participant-minute for 'streaming to a room'
summary: For a symmetric call (everyone talks and listens, few participants) the per-minute pricing model (RealtimeKit/LiveKit/Daily/Agora, all ~USD0.0004-0.002/participant-min) is simple and roughly comparable. For 'streaming audio to a room' -- one or few speakers, many silent listeners -- Cloudflare Realtime's flat USD0.05/GB egress does not multiply by listener minutes the way participant-minute billing implicitly does through per-connection bandwidth, so a large silent audience costs proportional to bytes sent, not headcount-times-time. Not independently benchmarked against real traffic; a reasoned inference from the billing units, not a vendor claim.

title: RealtimeKit has server-side recording: Start Recording API, per-track WebM
summary: RealtimeKit docs (start-recording, track-recording changelog 2026-05-28), fetched 2026-09-04: a Start Recording API returns a downloadUrl when composite recording completes; track-level recording creates a separate WebM file per participant instead of one composite, useful for post-processing, transcription and regulated/content-sensitive workflows. Answers the brief's question directly: yes, the SFU layer (via RealtimeKit) can record server-side -- client-side capture is not required.

title: The WebSocket adapter streams raw SFU media to your own Worker/DO for custom capture
summary: Changelog, 2026-05-29, fetched 2026-09-04: the SFU's WebSocket adapter streams WebRTC media to a standard WebSocket endpoint as PCM audio frames and JPEG video frames, in ingress or egress mode, consumable from Durable Objects, Workers, Containers or an external service, auto-reconnecting within a 5s window with buffering. This is the path for a custom recording/transcription pipeline that does not use RealtimeKit's built-in recorder.

title: Workers AI Whisper: USD0.0005/audio-minute, 10,000 free neurons/day
summary: workers-ai pricing page, dated 2026-08-28, fetched 2026-09-04: @cf/openai/whisper and @cf/openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo both USD0.0005 per audio minute (41-47 neurons/min). All Workers AI usage gets 10,000 free neurons/day on Free and Paid plans; beyond that USD0.011 per 1,000 neurons on Paid.

title: R2: USD0.015/GB-month; 32kbps Opus audio costs about USD0.0002/hour-month stored
summary: r2/pricing, fetched 2026-09-04: Standard storage USD0.015/GB-month, Class A ops USD4.50/M, Class B USD0.36/M, egress free (no data-transfer-out charge from R2, including via Workers/S3 API). Computed: 32kbps = 4KB/s = 14.06MB/hour = 0.0137GB/hour; one hour of audio stored for a month costs 0.0137 x USD0.015 = about USD0.0002. Storage cost for recorded chat audio is negligible next to transcription (Whisper) or SFU egress cost.

title: No searchable transcript index evaluated -- D1 FTS5 vs Workers AI embeddings + Vectorize
summary: The brief asks for a searchable transcript index; not investigated in depth this round. Two plausible Cloudflare-native paths: D1's SQLite FTS5 for keyword search over transcript text (cheap, exact-match/keyword only), or Workers AI embeddings + Vectorize for semantic search (higher cost per transcript, better recall). Neither was priced or prototyped here -- open for the next research pass.

title: US all-party-consent states: 12 by one count, but sources disagree on which 12
summary: recordinglaw.com (fetched 2026-09-04) lists 12: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Washington -- and flags Connecticut/Oregon as mixed (all-party only for phone calls or in-person, one-party for the other context), and Michigan as statutorily all-party but court-read as one-party since Sullivan v. Gray (1982). A different source's list swaps in Nevada for Oregon. No two sources agreed on the exact same 12 names; treat the count as 'about a dozen, genuinely contested at the edges,' not a clean list.

title: GDPR Art 17(3)(d)/Art 89: archival-public-interest exemption to erasure
summary: gdpr-info.eu, fetched 2026-09-04: Art 17(3)(d) exempts data from the right to erasure when processing is 'for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes... in so far as the right [to erasure] is likely to render impossible or seriously impair' that purpose (Art 89). Relevant to the brief's 'persistent public knowledge record' idea: a public archive of topic activity has a real legal path to resist erasure, but only with documented public-interest purpose and safeguards (restricted access, minimisation) -- not a blanket exemption.

title: GDPR Art 8: digital consent age is 16 by default, states may lower to 13
summary: gdpr-info.eu Art 8, fetched 2026-09-04, exact text: 'Where the child is below the age of 16 years, such processing shall be lawful only if... consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility... Member States may provide by law for a lower age... provided that such lower age is not below 13 years.' So the EU-wide minimum without parental consent varies 13-16 by member state -- there is no single EU number, unlike the US's flat COPPA 13.

title: COPPA 2.0 passed the Senate unanimously March 2026; still pending in the House
summary: Senator Markey's own press release plus independent reporting (Engadget), fetched 2026-09-04: the Senate unanimously passed the Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA 2.0) on 2026-03-06, extending protections from under-13 to under-17, with 13-16-year-olds able to consent for themselves (no parental consent required for that band). It has not passed the House as of this research; current law remains COPPA's under-13/parental-consent standard. Not yet enacted -- do not design against it as settled law.

title: Recommended consent default: no recording without explicit per-session opt-in, ever
summary: 12ish US all-party-consent states, GDPR's stricter baseline, and the unresolved erasure-vs-archive tension together argue for one default: recording (audio or transcript-as-recording-equivalent) is OFF unless every participant in a voice/video session explicitly opts in at session start, regardless of the participants' actual jurisdiction -- treat the product as all-party-consent everywhere. Text chat is not 'recording' in the same legal sense (it is the user's own typed speech, stored because the room stores messages) so it can default on for the public-record use case; voice/audio capture cannot.

title: Llama Guard 3 8B moderation: ~500ms latency, USD0.48/M input + USD0.03/M output tokens
summary: AI Gateway Guardrails docs, fetched 2026-09-04: 'evaluations using Llama Guard 3 8B on Workers AI add approximately 500 milliseconds per request'; longer content adds more, non-linearly. Model pricing page: USD0.48 per million input tokens, USD0.03 per million output tokens -- a short chat message (~100-200 tokens incl. a moderation prompt) costs a small fraction of a cent, but 500ms is too slow to gate every message before it appears.

title: Moderate async, not synchronously: 500ms is too slow to gate every message pre-send
summary: Given the ~500ms Llama Guard latency finding, gating every message before it reaches other users would double perceived chat latency at best. Recommend: send immediately, moderate in parallel, retract/flag on a rule violation (already how most chat platforms behave) -- reserve synchronous pre-send checks for higher-stakes actions (e.g. before starting a recording, before publishing to the public record). My inference from the latency number, not a documented CF or industry recommendation.

title: Rate limit, slow mode, mute/ban belong in the DO's own message handler, not a separate service
summary: durable-objects.md establishes DOs are single-threaded by construction: one object, one order, no locks. A per-channel DO already sees every inbound message in order before broadcasting, so slow-mode timers, per-user rate counters and a mute/ban set are plain in-memory state (rebuilt from ctx.getWebSockets() attachments per the doc's hibernation gotcha) checked inline before the broadcast loop -- no external rate-limiter or queue needed for a single-room MVP. Basis: public/imagine/stream/doc/durable-objects.md.

title: DO local-dev citation moved: durable-objects.md's url now 404s, current one confirmed
summary: The doc's local-development citation (developers.cloudflare.com/workers/development-testing/local-development/) now returns 404. Current page: developers.cloudflare.com/workers/local-development/, fetched 2026-09-04, confirms: 'Enabling remote connections for Durable Objects may be supported in the future, but currently will always run locally.' The doc's underlying claim holds; only the url needs updating.

title: Realtime SFU/TURN is NOT locally emulated -- it always hits the real Cloudflare edge
summary: Unlike Durable Objects (which run fully inside Miniflare/workerd with zero network calls), Cloudflare Realtime's SFU/TURN runs on every Cloudflare edge metal via anycast -- there is no local simulator for it. wrangler dev runs your own Worker code locally (the code that issues session tokens / calls the Realtime REST API), but actual media routing always goes to production Cloudflare infrastructure over the network, even in dev. This is a real asymmetry from the DO story worth calling out explicitly in the MVP doc.

title: Playwright supports multi-context WebRTC testing with fake media devices
summary: Chromium launch flags --use-fake-ui-for-media-stream (skip the permission prompt) and --use-fake-device-for-media-stream (feed getUserMedia a synthetic test pattern instead of a real camera/mic) let Playwright drive several browser contexts each with working fake audio/video, enabling automated multi-tab voice/video tests without real hardware. --use-file-for-fake-video-capture supplies a prepared file instead of the default pattern. Well-documented, widely used pattern; not CF-specific.

title: MVP recommendation: text-only, one hibernating DO per channel, one-line client change
summary: Text chat only for the MVP. One DO per channel (not per topic), SQLite-backed, Hibernation API, history in DO SQLite with a compaction alarm folding cold rows to R2 per durable-objects.md's shape. Client change is one line in Socket.js (swap window.location.host for the DO's url) plus swapping the JSONL byte-offset for a row id, both already opaque to the client per wire.md. No voice, no recording in the MVP -- first cost when voice is added is Realtime SFU's USD0.05/GB egress (1,000GB free/mo), not RealtimeKit's per-minute billing, unless the built-in recording/transcription/UI components are worth the extra cost.

title: Skeptic pass: what would falsify 'one DO per channel' as the right shape
summary: This recommendation would be wrong if channels are typically 1:1 DMs at huge scale (millions of near-empty DO instances is fine per 'unlimited objects,' but the per-object USD5/mo Workers Paid minimum is account-wide not per-object, so that is not the risk) -- the real falsifier would be a single wildly popular channel that legitimately needs more than ~1,000 req/sec or meaningfully more than 32,768 sockets, at which point per-channel sharding (multiple DOs per one logical channel, load-balanced) becomes necessary and the 'one DO per channel' rule needs a follow-up shape. Not observed in any cited source; flagging so the MVP doesn't treat this as permanently settled.
